name: Skin Wavelet Texture Analysis
description: Applies wavelet decomposition to skin texture regions for multi-scale pore and wrinkle pattern forensics.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated faces by analyzing skin texture at multiple scales using wavelet decomposition — real skin has characteristic frequency content at each scale that AI generators struggle to reproduce faithfully:

1. **Multi-Scale Wavelet Decomposition**: The method decomposes facial skin regions into frequency sub-bands using a 2D stationary wavelet transform (SWT) with Daubechies-4 wavelets across 5 decomposition levels. Each level produces three detail sub-bands (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) representing texture at different spatial frequencies: Level 1 captures the finest detail (pore-level texture, ~1–2 pixel features), Level 2 captures fine wrinkles and skin ridges (~2–4 pixels), Level 3 captures medium textural patterns (~4–8 pixels), Level 4 captures broader skin topology (~8–16 pixels), and Level 5 captures large-scale skin appearance (~16–32 pixels). For each sub-band, the method computes: coefficient magnitude histogram, kurtosis (peakedness), and inter-scale correlation.

2. **Natural Skin Texture Statistics**: Real skin texture follows predictable statistical patterns across wavelet scales. The key observations are: (a) wavelet coefficient distributions in skin regions follow a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD) with shape parameter β ≈ 0.5–0.8 (heavier tails than Gaussian), (b) inter-scale energy ratio follows a power law — each coarser level has approximately 2–4× less energy than the preceding level, (c) the ratio of horizontal-to-vertical detail energy reflects the anisotropy of skin texture (wrinkles tend to be horizontal on the forehead, radial around the eyes), (d) the kurtosis of Level 1 coefficients reflects pore density — higher kurtosis indicates sparser, more prominent pores. The method fits a GGD to each sub-band and measures deviation from expected parameters.

3. **AI Texture Artifact Detection**: AI-generated skin exhibits characteristic wavelet-domain artifacts: (a) spectral gaps — missing energy at specific scales, often at Level 1 (finest detail) where the generator's upsampling creates smooth, pore-free surfaces, (b) periodic patterns — GAN checkerboard artifacts appear as peaks in the wavelet coefficient histogram at regular intervals, (c) abnormal inter-scale correlation — real skin shows positive inter-scale correlation (large pores are surrounded by smaller pores), while AI skin may show zero or negative correlation, (d) isotropic texture — AI-generated skin often lacks the directional texture patterns (e.g., forehead furrows) present in real skin, showing equal energy in horizontal and vertical sub-bands when anisotropy is expected.

4. **Temporal Wavelet Consistency**: In video, the wavelet statistics of skin texture should remain stable across frames (skin texture doesn't change frame-to-frame). The method tracks the GGD shape parameter β and inter-scale energy ratio across frames for each facial region. Authentic video shows coefficient of variation < 0.05 for these parameters. AI-generated video often shows temporal fluctuations in wavelet statistics because the generator synthesizes slightly different texture in each frame — visible as a 'shimmering' or 'breathing' quality in the skin texture that manifests as coefficient variations > 0.2.
parameters:
Wavelet: Daubechies-4, stationary wavelet transform
Decomposition levels: 5
GGD shape parameter (authentic): β ≈ 0.5–0.8
Inter-scale energy ratio: 2–4× per level
Kurtosis analysis: Level 1 coefficients
Anisotropy ratio: horizontal/vertical energy
Temporal stability CV: < 0.05 (authentic)
Facial region segmentation: 68-point landmarks
Minimum skin patch: 64×64 pixels
Frame analysis window: 30 frames
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated faces via wavelet texture analysis. GGD parameter deviation achieves AUC of 0.87. Spectral gap detection provides F1-score of 0.85. Temporal consistency adds 3–5% improvement. Performance requires sufficient face resolution (> 200×200) and minimal compression (QP < 30).
source: Nataraj, L. et al. (2019). Detecting GAN Generated Fake Images Using Co-occurrence Matrices. IS&T Electronic Imaging, 532-1–532-7.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated faces through micro-texture frequency analysis. Identifying GAN checkerboard artifacts in skin regions. Forensic analysis of face swap detection at texture level. Quality assessment of face generation models.
strengths:
• Multi-scale analysis captures both fine and coarse texture anomalies
• GGD modeling provides a principled statistical framework
• Directional sub-bands detect anisotropy violations
• Temporal stability analysis exploits per-frame generation weakness
• Complementary to spatial-domain texture methods
limitations:
• Requires sufficient resolution for meaningful wavelet decomposition
• Heavy JPEG/video compression destroys high-frequency detail
• Cosmetic filters or beauty modes alter natural wavelet statistics
• Different skin types produce different baseline statistics
• Advanced generators with multi-scale discriminators may produce correct statistics
